description_full: J&J Snack Foods Corp. manufactures, markets, and distributes nutritional snack food and beverages to the food service and retail supermarket industries in the United States, Mexico, and Canada. The company operates through three segments: Food Service, Retail Supermarkets, and Frozen Beverages. It offers soft pretzels under the SUPERPRETZEL, SUPERPRETZEL BAVARIAN, NEW YORK PRETZEL, BAVARIAN BAKERY, FEDERAL PRETZEL, and BRAUHAUS brands, as well as under the private labels; frozen novelty under the DIPPIN'DOTS, LUIGI'S, WHOLE FRUIT, DOGSTERS, PHILLY SWIRL, ICEE, and MINUTE MAID brands; churros under the HOLA! and CALIFORNIA CHURROS brands; and handheld products under the private labels. The company also provides bakery products, such as fig and fruit bars, cookies, breads, rolls, crumbs, muffins, and donuts under the MRS. GOODCOOKIE, READI-BAKE, COUNTRY HOME, CAMDEN CREEK, MARY B'S, DADDY RAY'S and HILL & VALLEY brands, as well as under private labels; and frozen beverages under the ICEE, ARCTIC BLAST, SLUSH PUPPIE and PARROT ICE brands. In addition, it offers funnel cakes under the FUNNEL CAKE FACTORY brand, as well as various other food products; and sells machines and machine parts to other food and beverage companies. The company sells its products through a network of food brokers, independent sales distributors, and a direct sales force. It serves snack bars and food stand locations in chain, department and mass merchandising stores, malls and shopping centers, fast food and casual dining restaurants, stadiums and sports arenas, leisure and theme parks, convenience stores, movie theatres, warehouse club stores, schools, colleges and other institutions, and independent retailers. The company was incorporated in 1971 and is headquartered in Mount Laurel, New Jersey.

financial_summary: J & J Snack Foods Corp. is a small-cap consumer defensive business with a $1.7B market cap on $1.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +5% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 9% against a 7% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, with gross margins sitting at 30%.

The business throws off $82M in free cash flow — roughly 5 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.52× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 56× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 3.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 22% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.

mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 9% below the high.

val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $77.74 (margin of safety -16%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 7%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $62.88 to $100 (P10-P90).

Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 17% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 4.9% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.6% (vs the 8% bar).
The 2 covering analysts target $110 on average, 23% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 9% earns above the cost of capital of 7.1%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.36).
It runs a 30% gross margin and converts 5% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.52x.
ROE of 7% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.4x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $105.9M (6% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 4.9, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 4.7% over 3 years, 9.1% over 5 years and 5.0% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 56% of profits supports about 5.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 19.1% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.1x, 5.2% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 14, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 9.5% on average.
own: Insiders own 22.3%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 81%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (1 purchase).
It returns 3.8% a year to shareholders (0.2% in buybacks and 3.6% in dividends).
It pays out 124% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 12.9% of the float, 3.9 days to cover.
people: With about 4,600 employees, each generates about $344K of revenue, 0.7x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 5.5% a year.
That works out to $18K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $1.9M (6x revenue per employee).
